frames.narration: A new user signs up with the password 'hunter2'.
The application creates a random salt just for this user, then runs the slow password hash over the salt and the password.
Only the algorithm, the salt and the hash go into the database. The password itself is never stored or logged.
Later the user logs in. The application loads that user's salt and hash.
It hashes the typed password with the stored salt and compares the result with the stored hash in constant time. A match means the password is right.
Now an attacker steals the database. They see salts and hashes, not passwords. Every guess costs them the same slow hash, and every user must be attacked separately.
A strong, unique password still matters: a short or common one is guessed early whatever the hash. That is why logins also need rate limits and multi-factor authentication.
